The tensorlake npm SDK (v0.5.144) was backdoored with the Shai-Hulud self-propagating credential-stealing worm, targeting AI developer infrastructure by harvesting secrets across npm, AWS, Kubernetes, GitHub, and AI coding tools like Claude Code and VS Code.

Key findings:

- The compromise arrived via a rogue commit pushed to tensorlake's main branch on October 7, 2026 at 01:20 UTC under a maintainer's identity, with the malicious npm release following a day later. The attack chain begins at preinstall via a hook in package.json that executes package/lib/setup.mjs, an obfuscated loader that spawns the main worm, package/lib/Math_Symbol.js, using the Bun runtime. Defenders reviewing compromised CI logs should look for Bun process spawning during npm install steps.

- Shai-Hulud's payload is a broad-spectrum credential harvester: npm tokens, GitHub tokens, AWS credentials and secrets, HashiCorp Vault tokens, Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, .env files, cryptocurrency wallets, messaging app data, and config files tied to Anthropic Claude, Cursor, Kiro, Windsurf, and Zed. It also drops the HackBrowserData binary for browser credential extraction. Any secrets accessible to the process at install time should be considered compromised.

- The worm is self-propagating: it enumerates packages tied to the victim's npm publishing identity, builds Sigstore provenance, and republishes compromised versions to spread downstream. It also plants GitHub Actions workflows disguised as Copilot/Dependabot activity. Responders should audit the victim's entire npm publishing history and all associated GitHub Actions workflow files for unexpected additions.

- C2 resolution is blockchain-assisted: the worm queries an Ethereum smart contract to resolve its C2 endpoint at iseekaigogo[.]com, with GitHub used as a fallback staging location for encrypted exfiltrated data (look for public repos bearing the description "Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again"). The "hostage token" mechanism is particularly aggressive: a PowerShell monitor polls api.github[.]com/user on a loop using the stolen GitHub token, and if revocation is detected, it executes attacker-supplied code via Invoke-Expression, likely triggering a destructive routine. item.title: Credential Dumping using Windows Network Providers: How to Respond
item.description:
Credential dumping via rogue Windows Network Providers is a stealthy, LSASS-free technique that captures cleartext passwords at login, with almost no native hardening and limited AV/EDR coverage compared to Mimikatz or LSASS memory dumping.
Key findings:
- NPPSpy is the proof-of-concept tool at the center of this technique. A malicious DLL is dropped into %WINDIR%\System32 with admin rights, then registered as a Network Provider under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NPPSpy\NetworkProvider, and appended to the ProviderOrder value at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\NetworkProvider\Order. Once registered, every interactive logon causes Winlogon.exe to pass credentials through mpnotify.exe, which forwards cleartext credentials to every registered provider including the rogue DLL. Captured passwords land in C:\NPPSpy.txt in plaintext after each logon.
- The attack chain differs fundamentally from LSASS-based dumping. No LSASS handle is opened, no MiniDump is triggered, and none of the well-known comsvcs.dll, rdrleakdiag.exe, adplus.exe, dump64.exe, or sqldumper.exe abuse patterns apply. Because the credential capture happens inside a legitimate Windows authentication callback, many endpoint controls that watch for LSASS access simply have no visibility here.
- The registry is the primary forensic surface. The three legitimate ProviderOrder values are RDPNP, LanmanWorkstation, and WebClient. Any additional entry is anomalous. The corresponding DLL path is stored at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\[ProviderName]\NetworkProvider\ProviderPath. Skilled operators will rename the DLL to mimic a system file, so registry changes matter as much as the filename. The script Get-NetworkProviders.ps1 can enumerate all DLLs mpnotify is currently loading.
- Detection centers on registry write monitoring. The Elasticsearch query highlighted in the report watches registry.path matching HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet\Services\*\NetworkProvider\ProviderPath and flags any ProviderPath value that is not ntlanman.dll, drprov.dll, or davclnt.dll written by S-1-5-18. Any other entry warrants immediate investigation. Complementary hunts should look for unsigned or recently dropped DLLs in System32 alongside new service keys created in the same timeframe.
Takeaway: Baseline the ProviderOrder registry value now and alert on any modification. Hunt for non-default entries using Get-NetworkProviders.ps1, then correlate new System32 DLL drops with service key creation timestamps. If you find a rogue provider, preserve C:\NPPSpy.txt or whatever output file the DLL writes before remediation, that file is direct evidence of credential capture. Full detection query for Elasticsearch is in the report.
